camps.name: Eckernforde
camps.notes:
Goals: The top three priorities for each wind band: 
OFFSHORE wind. 
4-7 kts, 7-9, 9-11, 12-14 (and 22+). 
	Non-planing
	Marginal planing
	Full planing
	(Focusing on upwind sailing)

Overall: continuing to work on when it’s a shift and when it’s a change in pressure

4-7 kts

4-6 knots - non-planing
Paris:
1. Handle high enough to swing butt all the way in
2. Steering minimal, but anticipating headers with steering down
3. Eyes constantly out -talking about wind increase, decrease and duration
4. Pushing forward weight or testing weight on every opportunity

Helena: make sure handle is high enough.
1. Flat/slight windward heel - locked in, smooth.  4 kts: Me sitting in front of mast. 5-6 kts: Just starting to trap, with a foot on the mast, facing forward to anticipate next breeze (Feet move 1,2… 1,2)
2. Main trim: 4 kts: Flow mode. 5-6 kts: When clipped in: tight mainsheet, control the leech tension. Happy for leech telltales to stall more often. Range on mainsheet is very small, 1-2 clicks in/out. 
3. Keep glancing at jib telltales to be vocal in guiding the bow up or down, especially moments right after maneuvers

Other/both:
1. Stay in “the line” with weight
2. Move with shoulders first (also helps keep hips up to swing in fast)
3. Flatter setup: Kiwi or half kiwi setup

Tacking - Paris: 
- Keep weight low and unhook from bail
- Heel stays flat through the first half of the turn
- Widen stance when turning, back foot placement to grab new tiller extension
- Rotate body forward and pop battens from inside the boat (make sure handle high enough to allow this to happen) when bow is at optimal exit angle
	
Tacking - Helena:
- Keep mainsheet with me
- Move mainsheet inside lowers right away, as soon as Paris says “ready to tack”.
- Dead weight, minimal disturbance
- Unhook from bail, not the handle
- Mainsheet 6-8 inches or so eased when Paris pops battens, trimming in after that
- Urgency in looking at jib telltales right away for feedback on bow angle
- Working on improving my settle time in body position on new side


7 kts marginal-plane
Once we’re marginal planing, we’re trying our hardest to keep it as long as possible.
Goal is to keep boat going at a constant speed, accurate steering, trim, weight movements. Extremely precise.
“Protect the package”

Paris:
1. Hiking hard off inner rail or making step to outer rail with anticipation to step back in
2. Once we have the speed and flow we want - moving weight smaller increments to keep “the package”
3. Listening to Helena's bow down press to keep the package with eyes constantly out describing wind

Helena:
1. Keep glancing at jib telltales to direct the bow, be vocal and guide the press
2. Flat heel, minimal weight movements to protect “the package”. Feet will be either a foot on the mast or both feet in the middle of the front edge of the wing (mainsheet in front hand, aft hand to grab underneath outer wing). Facing forward to anticipate next puff or lull 
3. Main trim: Pulling mode, very small movements. Able to trim even tighter when boatspeed is fast, and on the breeze. Keep trim on when overspeed, “edge” = small eases when boatspeed drops, and then 1-2 clicks right back in. 



7-9 kts 
Marginal planing to full plane (9 kts)

Paris:
1. Handle high enough forward hiking - full stretch into shoulder straps
2. Hand on the toggle line to be ready for any pressure increase
3. Leaning into jib and calling for release to keep helm light (micro eases) once we have speed taking it for height
4. Talking about when we are no longer on VMG angle and anticipating a sharp aggressive turn down before header hits
5. Calling for conservative mode when wind looks turbulent 

Helena
1. Being vocal and urgent with “PRESS” calls while pressing hard into shoulder straps. This keeps boatspeed up, which keeps apparent wind up, which gives us more stability and more time to react.
- Microease to free up bow to press
- Cunno on just enough to take wrinkles out
2. Fore-aft leaning and small steps to control pitch with pressure changes
- Leaning forward for the initial hit of the puffs too, both feet on front corner of wing
- Once 9 kts, maybe small step aft
3. Conservative mode: not worried about the last 10%. Bank some leeward heel. Toggle up, get forward (front corner or front edge of wing), no over-easing. 
“Max trim” is an important call
4. Maneuvers: get forward ASAP. Front edge of wing when necessary

Other:
Full power - base setting




9-11 kts
Full plane

Paris
1. Constantly pressing into jib with no windward telltale “burn” to generate and keep speed
2. Chinese mode and constantly looking out calling wind increase, decrease and duration
3. Small steps forward and back depending on increase or decrease in pressure or moding

Helena
1. Using more cunningham to free up the bow
- Careful with this in tight lanes
- Vanging harder 
2. Pressing hard into shoulder straps, twisting to face forward, being vocal and urgent with “PRESS” call (no wwd telltale burning)
- Trimming with hands under trap bungee, feeding the chicken, hand over hand trimming in
3. Mainsheet range dependent on helm, mainsheet is rarely two-blocked 
- “Max trim” is an important call


12-14 kts

Paris
1. Chinese mode all the time - making sure I am shoulder to shoulder with Helena
2. Constantly looking out calling wind increase, decrease and duration
3. Aggressive bow down before headers (precise steering and relying on Helena for this)
4. Calling for release if helm feels heavy or right before a header puff
5. Trimming jib harder 

Helena
1. Chinese mode, using forward lean to stay stable through pressure changes
- Fully trapping low
- Stepping slightly further back for low mode (getting over the fleet etc)
2. Anticipating headers and lifts - 
Header puff - feed the chicken to release the bow to accept the header
Lifting puff - less initial ease, then watch for the backside (eventual header) - need small release to press again for oncoming header
Lulls - leaning forward, maybe small step forward, slight trim and heel
(Continuing to press as boatspeed/apparent wind builds, “speed build header”)
3. Main trim: small, frequent movements. Fight the tendency to overease or overtrim. Offshore breeze - there will be times the mainsheet is out of range. Cunno and vang adjustments as needed for moding and keeping main in range most of the time. 

“Hold the main” = don’t trim in yet, let the bow find where it needs to go


22+ kts

Paris:
1. Chinese mode - hiking farther back, but higher on trapeze toggle for windward heel 
2. Trimming jib really tight to allow bow to be closer to the wind to help with windward heel
3. Steering mode - steering a lot more keeping arm close to body 
4. Right now helping Helena with “sneaking it in” moments 
5. Calling big pressure (most likely headers) aggressively steering bow down before header and telling her when rudder is too loaded
6. Deep breaths being present

Helena
1. Chinese mode hiking HARD
- May be toggled up for windward heel
2. Mainsheet trimming technique - sailing on the jib, main just follows…keeping a pretty light load in main
- Always ready for a fast ease or trim
- Really important to ease quickly just before/as the puff hits
- Mechanics: Eases = Feed the chicken, Trims = ladder (hand over hand)
- Identifying the moments to “Sneak it in” (proactive to take out slack)
- Pace: Small movements often/constantly, ease then right back in, trim then right back out
3. Max cunno, accurate vang setting 
Vang may be a little too tight for the very biggest puffs but that’s better than too little most of the time…
4. Racing: keep it clean and simple, no one has the boat in range 100% of the time, deep breaths, racing is about steady boathandling and laylines


“Chinese mode” = Hiking super hard and stable upwind:
Leaning forward
Pressing into shoulder straps
Rigid and straight legs, (especially back leg) tight glutes
Weight balanced between two feet to stay stable, on toes
Twisting to face further upwind 
Head down, not lifted (neck straight)
Mainsheet under trap bungee
Paris will be right next to me, looks like “one person”


Upwind tactics and positioning Notes:

East - South East wind
Near the left shore line
10-14knots

Left pressure and angle won the majority of the day, but could get away with the gybe set if in pack. pick left mark looking downwind and tack to ensure you are going back left for the upwind beat if you gybeset. If you aren’t going left you need to be going to the edge right. 

Starting:
Pin most boat fighting for EDGE won - few more higher lines from pin worked, but only a couple. Need to be able to hold off line to 85% left. sessions.rawStandardMove:
2 races in NNE breeze. 350-30º.  5-17kts.  Course 2 off point of land.
3rd race in filling breeze from W.  285º.  4-12kts.  Course 3 by C'an Pastilla.

NNE wind (course 2).  Was characterized by strong righties from Arenal and more gentle, but big, lefties from Palma.  Was a day to get to your side and then pick best lane back to middle.  
We gained by pushing more to corner as well as taking Tim's lane earlier.  It all depended on how the wind was looking more long term, and if it was sustained good to dig, if not maybe look to connect back to what was paying.  There were many shifts per beat, so not getting to lay line was usually good.  Downwind was open, but seemed good to just attack pressure.  Was not always easy to see.

W wind (course 3).  Similar to the final day of MSC regatta.  We wanted to look at the right but with a knowledge of shifts/pressure/finish top left.  Started middle of line and held in righty pressure, got nervous it wasn't going to come back, but in the end there was always something good about not being on STBD lay line.  Going straight downwind was also good.  Both in MSC regatta and this race.

We did a good job consolidating/protecting when we needed to and were unsure.

standardMoves.description:
Wind was from 35-60º or so.  9-16kts.  Some upwind waves, but mostly shifty offshore conditions.  We said this would be a condition each side would win.  Wind was a little to the right of 90º to the beach, which seemed to help the right have more wind since there was more clear water that way.

We did a nice job of balancing when to go back to corner for more, and when to leave early and be prepared for an oscillation back the other way.

On upwind it seemed strong to be to windward approaching the corner so you could see the progression of the other boats and make your decision of when to leave that side.  When you are leading to the corner (the low boat) you don't always get to see how strong or weak you are on little shifts that would be good times to cross.

Downwind, gybe set was almost always strong but I was pretty cold and the boat handling made it hard to always trust in the gybe set, because I was pretty tangled at the top mark sometimes.

standardMoves.description:
2 races in NNE breeze. 350-30º.  5-17kts.  Course 2 off point of land.
3rd race in filling breeze from W.  285º.  4-12kts.  Course 3 by C'an Pastilla.

NNE wind (course 2).  Was characterized by strong righties from Arenal and more gentle, but big, lefties from Palma.  Was a day to get to your side and then pick best lane back to middle.  
We gained by pushing more to corner as well as taking Tim's lane earlier.  It all depended on how the wind was looking more long term, and if it was sustained good to dig, if not maybe look to connect back to what was paying.  There were many shifts per beat, so not getting to lay line was usually good.  Downwind was open, but seemed good to just attack pressure.  Was not always easy to see.

W wind (course 3).  Similar to the final day of MSC regatta.  We wanted to look at the right but with a knowledge of shifts/pressure/finish top left.  Started middle of line and held in righty pressure, got nervous it wasn't going to come back, but in the end there was always something good about not being on STBD lay line.  Going straight downwind was also good.  Both in MSC regatta and this race.

We did a good job consolidating/protecting when we needed to and were unsure.
standardMoves.name: 2 races in NNE breeze.

standardMoves.description:
Northerly 8-15kts.  Race course 3 close to C'an Pastilla again.

We did a nice job of staying in phase but at least "touching" the best pressure.  Worked nicely for us to not always dig deep into pressure but rather get on the lifted tack ASAP because it was such a shifty day.  3-5 shifts per beat.

Downwind we still did a nice job attacking best pressure out of WW mark.  However, a few times we gybed early thinking we were sailing out of pressure when no one was really threatening us from behind and we can continue a little longer and close down the corner.  If bows are still pointing on our line behind us on downwind that is another indication there is not much rush.

We don't always need to gybe against the shift downwind (TP52 race Valencia example).  Sometimes best to just go get that header and worry about the lift back to the mark later, not usually a problem in the 49er.  Not as much as keelboats.
standardMoves.name: Northerly 8-15kts.
